Factors that matter most in choosing the right CRM when outgrowing Pipedrive. While all featured options offer SaaS-only deployment, cost models range from flat subscriptions to per-seat tiers and custom pricing, directly affecting total cost predictability as your team scales. For businesses needing deep customization, significant cost reduction, or flexible hosting, including the option to host on your own infrastructure, standard SaaS alternatives may fall short. Ditch your expensive CRM subscription Get a custom CRM designed for your workflow at a fraction of the price. Talk to our team to get a fixed quote. Book a call For custom workflows & infrastructure: Miniloop For businesses that have outgrown the limits of off-the-shelf CRMs, Miniloop stands alone as a fully custom CRM solution. Unlike Pipedrive or any SaaS competitor, Miniloop is architected to fit your unique business processes rather than forcing your operations to adapt to generic modules or sales pipelines. Every implementation is a clean-slate build, tailored from the ground up to your specifications. Delivering a system that matches the exact way your team works, from deal flows to compliance steps to role-specific automation. A major departure from standard CRM pricing models, Miniloop completely eliminates per-seat fees. Your annual price covers the initial buildout, all ongoing support, and future updates. Whether your team is 10 users or 500, you aren’t penalized for growth or adoption. This approach is particularly meaningful for large organizations or those with fluctuating headcounts, who often see subscription costs balloon unexpectedly with traditional vendors. Another layer of flexibility comes with Miniloop’s infrastructure options. Customers can choose fully managed cloud hosting or run the solution on their own hardware. Ideal for organizations that must meet regional data regulations or policy-driven infrastructure standards. With this control, you aren’t locked into any vendor’s ecosystem, and your data remains portable, giving true ownership and easy migration capabilities. Full data migration is baked into every Miniloop engagement. Rather than leaving you with siloed records or broken workflows, Miniloop specialists ensure all critical customer, deal, and interaction data comes across from legacy CRMs. Custom workflows, field mappings, and permissions are reconstructed to match your actual processes, not a lowest-common-denominator template. Who sees the most ROI with Miniloop? The gains are clearest for high-expenditure teams, especially those spending $50,000 per year or more on CRM licenses across multiple departments or brands. Process-driven organizations with regulated workflows, such as those in finance, healthcare, or legal, benefit from being able to specify logic for every record, approval, and security requirement. Compliance-focused buyers, where infrastructure choice and auditability are paramount, finally get a solution built to their standards rather than accepting “close enough” from SaaS best-fits. There are important limits to consider. Miniloop is not built for small teams with basic CRM needs who are well-served by out-of-the-box solutions. It isn’t a self-serve SaaS that can be trialed and switched out in a day. Successful engagements require a consultative approach and an investment in defining workflows and operational requirements up front. And while Miniloop is highly customizable, it is not a direct answer to all-in-one marketing automation platforms; its strength is in core CRM and workflow fit. Choosing Miniloop is a strategic decision for organizations that view CRM as business-critical infrastructure, not just a SaaS tool. It offers a path out of per-seat pricing, enables deep customization, and puts ownership of systems and data back in your control. Something no generic CRM on this list can match. For deep enterprise customization: Salesforce Salesforce stands out as the market’s most powerful enterprise CRM, offering unrivaled breadth across sales, service, marketing, and operations modules, backed by deep customization and an expansive third-party ecosystem. For organizations with complex needs and the IT resources to support them, Salesforce provides the tools to architect business processes that fit almost any requirement. But carries significant cost and complexity, from seat-based pricing to ongoing administration. Salesforce’s platform goes far beyond basic deal and contact management. Its suite includes Sales Cloud for pipeline tracking, Service Cloud for customer support, Marketing Cloud for multi-channel campaigns, and modules for everything from billing to workforce management. Each of these products can be deployed individually or combined, supporting businesses that need full end-to-end visibility and coordination across functions. This allows large teams to consolidate disparate tools and operate from a unified data layer. A defining advantage for Salesforce is its extensive customization capabilities. Administrators and developers can tailor workflows, automate business processes, and define custom fields to mirror even the most intricate organizational structures. The platform’s declarative tools, for example, the drag-and-drop Flow Builder, let non-technical users automate tasks and build approval chains, while the integrated Apex programming language enables nearly limitless backend logic for development teams. As a result, enterprises can mold Salesforce to accommodate highly specialized sales cycles, compliance needs, or reporting requirements that generic CRMs struggle to support. The AppExchange marketplace is another Salesforce hallmark. It serves as an ecosystem of thousands of pre-built applications and connectors, ranging from e-signature solutions to AI analytics and industry-specific modules. This breadth of third-party support enables rapid expansion of core functionality. Organizations can find vetted add-ons to fill gaps or extend Salesforce into areas like accounting, HR, or field services, reducing the need for completely custom builds. However, the depth Salesforce offers comes with substantial trade-offs. Pricing is typically seat-based, which means costs increase with each user added. This can quickly escalate for growing teams, especially when factoring in necessary add-ons and premium integrations. Many of which are only available at higher tiers or via AppExchange partners. For instance, what starts as a core CRM deployment often expands to include additional modules, each incurring separate fees. Implementation and ongoing management also pose challenges. Deploying Salesforce often requires both in-house IT expertise and third-party consultants to handle data migration, process design, and training. Many organizations find the initial rollout demanding, with a lengthy onboarding curve as workflows are adapted and users are brought up to speed. After launch, the platform’s advanced features and constant updates necessitate ongoing administration, sometimes justifying the need for dedicated Salesforce admins or developers. This added resource burden can be daunting for companies lacking extensive IT staff. Compounding these challenges, the flexibility that powers Salesforce’s customization can also complicate maintenance. Custom-built workflows and integrations may create dependencies that make future upgrades or migrations more complex. Teams considering a transition away from Salesforce later often cite entanglement with bespoke automations and fields as a key inhibitor. For large enterprises and organizations where process complexity and integration are non-negotiable, Salesforce remains the go-to choice. Its robust ecosystem and infrastructure suit companies willing to invest in a scalable, extensible platform. Provided they accept the requisite commitments in cost, time, and technical overhead. To learn how other solutions handle pricing transparency and admin overhead, see our analysis of Zendesk pricing for another enterprise tool with layered costs and options. For all-in-one sales & marketing: HubSpot CRM HubSpot CRM stands out as the best option for mid-size businesses and growing sales teams that want an all-in-one platform for sales, marketing automation, and customer data. With fast onboarding and smooth integration between email, pipelines, and reporting. Its bundled approach provides simplicity and powerful native inbound marketing features, making it a popular pick for organizations prioritizing ease of use over deep customization or infrastructure control. HubSpot’s core differentiator is its unified platform, where marketing automation, sales management, and analytics all live under one roof. Teams can easily build and execute inbound campaigns with HubSpot’s drag-and-drop email builder, forms, landing pages, and integrated blog tools. Sales reps manage deals in visual pipelines, automating repetitive tasks through simple workflows. Native reporting lets managers tie lead sources to revenue, track conversion rates, and spot pipeline bottlenecks. All without requiring third-party integrations or custom development. Onboarding with HubSpot is straightforward; many SMBs and midsize firms can go live in days, not weeks. The user interface is clean and intuitive, minimizing training needs for new reps or marketers. This is a key reason why HubSpot is frequently recommended for teams transitioning from siloed tools or spreadsheets: sales, marketing, and support operate off shared data, reducing confusion and duplicate work. A defining strength is the platform’s inbound marketing engine. HubSpot was built with content-driven lead generation at its core. Features like automated nurture sequences, lead scoring, blog SEO recommendations, and detailed page analytics are native, allowing marketing teams to execute campaigns without technical bottlenecks. This is especially useful for organizations focusing on driving website traffic, capturing leads, and converting them into deals. A demand that’s grown as outbound tactics evolve. For context on tools specializing in lead enrichment and outreach, see our reviews on Orbitly and Hunter.io . However, the core advantage, the tightly integrated bundle, can also become a double-edged sword. While the all-in-one design reduces tool sprawl, it also increases the risk of lock-in. As organizations grow or their needs shift, any change (like switching to a specialized reporting system or custom workflow) must be weighed against the disruption of migrating all contact history, automations, and landing pages away from the HubSpot ecosystem. Many teams stick with HubSpot longer than planned due to the complexity of moving critical business data out. Pricing is another major consideration. HubSpot CRM starts free, but essential automation, reporting, and pipeline features are locked behind tiered, per-seat paid plans. Costs can climb quickly for teams with multiple sales reps or active marketing campaigns. Upgrading for features like lead scoring, advanced analytics, or custom reporting often moves companies into higher-priced packages, impacting long-term ROI. Customization is where HubSpot shows clear limits. While it’s possible to use workflows to automate simple tasks and adjust pipelines, the platform is not built for niche industries or organizations needing highly specialized processes. Teams with unique approval flows, multi-stage deal management, or non-standard data models may find the configuration point-and-click friendly but ultimately constrained. No deep code-level changes, no off-platform data hosting, and no true infrastructure flexibility. HubSpot CRM is well-suited for midsize organizations after a frictionless, unified sales and marketing platform, prioritizing ease of use and built-in inbound tools over deep customization or infrastructure independence. The bundle streamlines go-to-market operations but requires a careful look at long-term lock-in, per-seat costs, and limits for teams eyeing tailored workflows or full control over their CRM environment. For automation on a budget: Zoho CRM Zoho CRM is the top choice for businesses prioritizing affordable, feature-rich automation over the higher costs of Pipedrive or all-in-one suites like Salesforce. Its competitive monthly pricing, automation depth, and configurable workflows make it stand out for budget-conscious SMBs ready to streamline leads and customer communication without sacrificing much power. Positions typically reserved for higher-priced tools. The platform’s extensive ecosystem of add-ons allows companies to extend CRM utility into inventory, finance, and project work without expensive migrations. It’s particularly effective for teams that want automation and flexibility but aren’t ready to manage or pay for an enterprise-grade solution. Weaknesses: Zoho’s support responsiveness can lag compared to premium vendors, and the UI, while functional, feels less polished than competitors like HubSpot or Salesforce. Some users find the breadth of features can be overwhelming, with a steeper configuration curve, especially as more add-ons are deployed. Choose Zoho CRM when: You want end-to-end sales automation, flexible workflow design, and customizable modules. Without the budget strain of tools like Salesforce or Pipedrive. It’s ideal for SMBs scaling up from spreadsheet-based processes or outgrowing limited free CRMs, but who don’t need highly specialized enterprise features or the most intuitive UI. If tight integration with tools for finance, project management, or customer support is a must, Zoho CRM’s ecosystem is hard to match at its price point. For teams considering automation at the ground-up level, Zoho is one of the most cost-effective launchpads available. For affordable sales automation: Freshsales Freshsales offers sales teams a budget-friendly CRM with built-in phone and email tools, simple automation for outreach, and AI lead scoring, making it a top pick for small businesses and fast-growing teams who want integrated sales automation at a competitive price. While Freshsales delivers effective sales productivity out of the box, it lacks the deep workflow customization required by highly specialized or niche organizations. Best for: Affordable sales automation and small team CRM Key features: Built-in cloud telephony and email tracking, allowing reps to contact leads directly within the CRM AI-based lead scoring that identifies hot prospects and prioritizes follow-up efforts Visual sales pipelines and deal tracking to manage progress at a glance Customizable email sequences and workflow automation for lead nurturing Integration across the Freshworks suite, facilitating shared data with helpdesk, marketing, and chat apps Useful onboarding materials and responsive support resources for quick adoption Pricing: Growth plan: $15/user/month with core CRM and automation features Pro plan: $39/user/month adding deeper analytics and some customizations Custom enterprise pricing for advanced needs and large teams Strengths: Freshsales stands out for integrating telephony, email, and pipeline management in a single, clean interface, greatly reducing the need for third-party add-ons. Simpler onboarding and user support make it practical even for non-technical teams or managers aiming for a swift rollout. Its AI tools for lead scoring and basic workflow automation are highly accessible, giving small businesses a solid entry-point into sales automation. Weaknesses: Companies with complex or unusual sales processes may find Freshsales’ workflow automations somewhat limited. Deeply nuanced triggers, conditional logic, or highly customized data fields are more constrained compared to larger enterprise platforms. Teams tied into broader non-Freshworks ecosystems could hit integration walls, and feature expansion is typically tied to per-user upgrades. Choose Freshsales when: You need a cost-effective CRM that covers essential sales automation, calling, emailing, pipeline tracking, without heavy IT involvement or configuration. It’s a strong fit for growing sales teams who prize approachability and don’t require advanced tailoring. If you’re scaling rapidly and want to avoid paying for features you won’t use, Freshsales delivers reliable automation at a predictable monthly rate. Insightly leads in project-based scalability, Nutshell enables easy team collaboration for basic pipelines, and ClickUp prioritizes workflow management over traditional CRM. title: Why Your Bank Reconciliation Process Breaks Before It Even Starts
summary: Bank reconciliation stalls in multi entity environments not because matching is complex but because the data assembly required to begin matching arrives fragmented and inconsistent.
body_text: The Real Problem Isn't Reconciliation. It's What Comes Before It. The standard assumption is that reconciliation delays come from volume or complexity. They do not. They come from the data collection that happens before the first match is attempted. Controllers managing multiple entities and bank accounts spend the opening phase of every reconciliation cycle gathering transaction data from separate bank portals, exporting it in different formats, and organizing it into a structure the ERP or reconciliation tool can consume. The bank reconciliation process is technically straightforward. The preparation required to begin it is not. Our team estimates that 30% to 50% of total reconciliation cycle time is spent on data assembly rather than actual transaction matching. Every Entity Adds a Reconciliation Silo In a single-entity environment, the controller matches one bank feed against one ledger. In a multi-entity structure, every legal entity carries its own set of bank accounts, its own chart of accounts, and often its own GL timing. Intercompany transactions add another layer, where a transfer out of one entity should appear as a transfer into another but frequently posts on different dates or under different reference codes. Account reconciliation across entities becomes a coordination exercise that depends on every feed arriving on time, in the right format, and with enough detail to match against the corresponding ledger entries. Reconciliation across entities is not parallel processing. It is sequential dependency. Transaction Matching Fails on Inconsistency, Not Volume Most reconciliation tools match well when inputs are clean and uniform. The problem is they rarely are. One bank includes remittance detail in the transaction description. Another truncates it. A third lumps multiple payments into a single settlement entry. Controllers handling transaction matching across banks are not just matching amounts. They are interpreting how each bank chose to represent the same financial event. We often see teams maintaining 5 to 15 bank-specific matching rules to compensate for these inconsistencies, each requiring manual updates when a bank changes its output format. Where the Financial Close Process Absorbs the Delay The ripple effect moves downstream quickly: Reconciliation exceptions that require manual investigation hold open line items past the soft close deadline Intercompany eliminations stall because one entity's bank transactions have not been fully matched while the counterparty's have Controllers escalate unresolved items to the next period rather than delay the close, creating a rolling backlog that compounds monthly The financial close process does not slow down because of accounting judgment. It slows down because the inputs needed to exercise that judgment arrive late and inconsistently. Close delays are rarely accounting problems. They are data availability problems. Centralized Visibility Removes the Preparation Step The pattern that breaks reconciliation at scale is decentralized data collection. When every entity's bank data flows through a separate channel into a separate staging area, the controller becomes the integration layer. A platform like Arpari centralizes transaction data across all banks and entities into a single normalized view, so reconciliation starts from a consistent, already-organized dataset. Transaction formats are standardized at the point of ingestion, not at the point of matching. The bank reconciliation process shifts from a data preparation exercise to an exception management exercise, which is where controller expertise delivers the most value. Key Takeaways The bank reconciliation process stalls in multi-entity environments not because matching is complex but because the transaction data required to begin matching arrives fragmented and inconsistent. Controllers absorb this gap by manually assembling and normalizing bank data before reconciliation can start, which compresses the time available for actual investigation and resolution. Account reconciliation improves most when the preparation step is eliminated, not optimized. Centralizing bank transaction data into a single layer gives controllers a complete, standardized starting point and returns cycle time back to the close. The fastest reconciliation is the one that does not wait for the data to be ready. See it in action Welcome to the next level of clarity from Arpari. Want to try it live? Book a 30-minute demo at www.arpari.com/demo to see how Arpari normalizes bank data at ingestion so reconciliation starts from a complete, consistent dataset. Arpari is the modern treasury platform for real estate owners, operators, and finance teams. We aggregate bank data, automate cash reporting, and now let you move money securely, across every bank, in one workspace. ‍

title: NAIC Life Insurance Locator: A Practitioner's Guide (August 2026)
summary: Find out how to submit an NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator request in August 2026, including what information you need to gather beforehand.
body_text: When determining if a decedent had a life insurance policy, the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator is one of the best free tools available to help. It sends an alert to participating insurers, who then check their own records for a match. If they find one, they contact you directly. This guide covers how to use the NAIC locator, who qualifies to submit a request, and what information to gather. Key Takeaways The NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator is a free search service that alerts participating insurers to check records for a deceased person's policies. You need legal standing to submit a request: either as a named beneficiary or someone with authority over the estate. Insurers have 90 days to respond, and silence after that window generally means no match among participating companies. You can submit without a Social Security number using the decedent's name, date of birth, and last known state of residence, though responses may take longer. Elayne handles the broader asset search alongside the administrative steps that follow a death, including financial accounts and survivor benefits. What the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator Is The NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator is a free, centralized search service run by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners. It lets families search for life insurance policies and annuity contracts that may have been purchased by someone who has since died. When a search request is submitted, participating insurers receive an alert and check their records against the deceased's information. If a match is found, the insurer contacts the potential beneficiary directly. The service covers policies from insurers who have opted in, which represents a broad share of the market. {{blog-cta-attorneys}} Who Can Use the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator The service is free and open to the public, with no login required. Beneficiaries , estate administrators, executors, trustees, and attorneys can all submit requests on behalf of a deceased person's estate. Two conditions must be met before submitting. First, the person whose policies you are searching for must be deceased. The NAIC locator is built for post-death searches and will not surface benefits from policies held by someone who is still living. Second, you must have standing to request the information: you are either a named beneficiary on the policy or someone with legal authority over the estate, such as an executor or court-appointed administrator. Insurers only respond to parties with a legitimate claim or legal right to the information. What Information You Need Before Submitting a Request Your own details Your legal first and last name Your current mailing location Your email The deceased's details These should come directly from the death certificate : Legal first and last name Date of birth Date of death Social Security number (SSN), or an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) if the deceased was not eligible for an SSN Step-by-Step: How to Submit a Request The NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator is free to use and accessible here . Here is what to gather before you begin: The full legal name of the deceased, including any name variations or maiden names they may have used over their lifetime, since insurers search their records using exactly the name provided. The Social Security number of the deceased, which is the primary identifier insurers use to match records. Date of birth and date of death, both of which help narrow results when common names are involved. Your own contact information, including a valid email, because all insurer responses are sent to you directly instead of through the NAIC portal. Once you have gathered that information, the submission process follows these steps: Going to the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator and creating a free account using your email. There is no login app; the service runs entirely through a web browser. Completing the online request form with the deceased's identifying details. The form also asks for your relationship to the deceased and your contact information. Submitting the request. NAIC then forwards it to all participating insurers, each of which searches its own records independently. Waiting for insurer responses. Participating companies have 90 days to respond, though many reply sooner. Responses arrive by email or mail directly from each insurer, not from NAIC itself. If an insurer locates a policy or annuity contract in the deceased's name, they will contact you with instructions for filing a claim. What Happens After You Submit a Request After submitting a request through the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator, the process moves into a matching phase that can take up to 90 business days. Participating insurers receive the submission and search their records for any policies or annuity contracts that name the person as an insured or owner. If a match is found, the company contacts the requestor directly, not through NAIC. Other Free Policy Locator Resources to Use Alongside the NAIC Tool The NAIC tool is a strong starting point, but it only reaches insurers who have opted into the service. Here are other locator resources worth checking: Resource Cost Coverage NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator Free Participating insurers MIB Group Locator $75 per search Member-insurer records back to 1996 State insurance department programs Free State-licensed insurers NAUPA / state unclaimed property databases Free Lapsed or unpaid policy proceeds escheated to the state Employer HR department Free Group life coverage tied to employment Searching Without a Social Security Number or With Limited Information The NAIC locator asks for a Social Security number , but submitting a request without one is still possible. The search form includes a field for partial information, and NAIC reviewers can work with a name, date of birth, and last known state of residence when no SSN is available. For searches without a Social Security number, the following details strengthen the request: Full legal name at the time the policy was issued, including any name changes or maiden names that may appear on older policies. Date of birth and, if known, the date of death for a deceased individual, since insurers match records against both. Last known state of residence, which helps narrow the search to insurers licensed in that jurisdiction. Any partial policy information, such as an insurer name, agent name, or approximate policy year. Searches by name alone take longer to process and may return fewer matches, since insurers rely on SSN as the primary identifier. {{blog-cta-attorneys}} How Elayne Supports the Broader Search for Life Insurance and Estate Assets The NAIC locator is a strong starting point, but life insurance policies are only one part of what families often need to locate after a loss. Unclaimed bank accounts, forgotten investment accounts, and lapsed annuities may exist as well. Elayne is designed to handle this broader asset search alongside the administrative steps that follow a death. This includes searching for financial accounts, notifying institutions, and coordinating survivor benefits. FAQ Can I use the NAIC life insurance policy locator for a living person? The NAIC life insurance policy locator is built for post-death searches and will not surface active policy benefits for someone who is still alive. What's the best free life insurance policy locator for finding a deceased parent's policies? The NAIC life insurance policy locator is the strongest free starting point: it reaches a broad range of participating insurers at no cost and requires no login app. Running a parallel search through your state's unclaimed property database and submitting a request to MIB Group can help cover policies the NAIC service may miss, since no single locator reaches every insurer. How do I search for a life insurance policy by name when I don't have a Social Security number? You can submit the request through the NAIC life insurance policy locator using the deceased's full legal name, date of birth, date of death, and last known state of residence; the form accepts partial information when no SSN is available. Name-only searches take longer and may return fewer matches because participating insurers use the SSN as their primary identifier. NAIC life insurance policy locator vs. MIB life insurance policy locator: which should I use first? One option is to start with the NAIC locator because it is fully free, reaches a wide range of participating insurers, and returns results within 90 business days. The MIB life insurance policy locator costs $75 per search, but searches member-insurer records going back to 1996 and can help surface policies the NAIC tool may not identify. Is the NAIC life insurance policy locator legitimate? Yes. The NAIC (the National Association of Insurance Commissioners) is the U.S. standard-setting body for state insurance regulation, and the locator is a free, official service it operates on behalf of families searching for unclaimed policies. Insurers who participate are required to search their own records and respond directly to requestors within 90 days, making it one of the most credible free tools available for a post-death life insurance policy search by name or Social Security number. *Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not provide legal, medical, financial, or tax advice. title: Does AvePoint Back Up Google Workspace?
summary: Learn how AvePoint backs up Google Workspace with automated protection, granular restore, and independent recovery beyond Google Vault and native retention limits.
body_text: Yes, AvePoint backs up Google Workspace. AvePoint provides automated backup for Gmail, Google Drive and Shared Drives, Calendar, Chat, Directory Users and Groups, Contacts, Forms, and Google Classroom, with granular and bulk restore. This closes the gaps in Google’s own retention tools, which only manually recover deleted data in limited scenarios and are not designed to function as a backup at all. Key Takeaways AvePoint backs up Google Workspace. AvePoint’s backup capabilities cover Gmail, Google Drive and Shared Drives, Calendar, Chat, Directory Users and Groups, Contacts, Forms, and Google Classroom, with granular and bulk restore. Google Vault is a retention and eDiscovery tool, not a backup. It governs data in place and keeps no separate, restorable copy. Native recovery windows expire in roughly 25 days. After which, Google’s own tools can’t restore permanently deleted data at all. Vault holds may not preserve all shared content. Files shared only indirectly through an alias or Google Group rather than directly with a user’s account may not be preserved by a Vault hold. Many organizations run Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 together. AvePoint backs up both under one platform. AI-powered tools are only as reliable as the data behind them. As Gemini searches and summarizes across Gmail and Drive, backup gaps become a data-quality gap for every AI answer built on that content. A backup is only as effective as its recovery process. Test your restore process before an incident forces you to test it live. Why Does Google Workspace Need Independent Backup? Google Workspace needs independent backup because its native recovery windows expire in days, not years, and Google Vault, its retention and eDiscovery tool, explicitly does not function as a backup. Vault governs data in place inside Google Workspace. It doesn’t create a separate copy, so if a file is corrupted, encrypted by ransomware, or purged after its retention window, the version Vault manages is affected too. Google’s own documentation is direct about this distinction. Google Vault is built for retention and eDiscovery, and Google’s own retention documentation confirms that once retention rules expire, messages are removed from a user’s view, with only a limited additional window that varies by service for a Vault administrator to search, export, or place a hold on them before they’re gone for good. Short, hard recovery windows. The Admin console can restore recently deleted Drive and Gmail data only within roughly 25 days, deleted Contacts within about 30 days via Contacts Trash, and a deleted user’s entire data set within about 20 days, after which native tools cannot restore the data at all. Vault is not a backup. Google Vault keeps no independent copy of your data and offers very limited options for restoring content directly to end users. Gaps in scope. Files shared with a user via an alias or Google Group (rather than directly with their account) may not be preserved by a Vault hold. No help after admin compromise. If an admin account is compromised, or the retention window has already expired, native tools and Vault can’t restore what’s gone. How Does AvePoint Back Up Google Workspace? AvePoint backs up Google Workspace with automated protection across Gmail, Google Drive and Shared Drives (including metadata and permissions), Calendar, Chat, Directory Users and Groups, Contacts, Forms, and Google Classroom with self-service restore through its ReCenter portal. What’s protected: Gmail, Google Drive and Shared Drives (including file metadata and permissions), Calendar, Chat, Directory (User and Groups), Forms, Calendar (past and future events), Contacts, and Google Classroom (grades, assignments, documents, users, and announcements) Restore: Granular or bulk search and restore Google Workspace data with self-service capabilities through the ReCenter portal Backup frequency: Automated, running up to four times a day, rather than relying on Google’s own trash and retention windows Storage: Unlimited cloud storage with a choice of over a dozen global data centers, including Azure, Google Cloud Platform (GCP), Amazon Web Services (AWS), and bring your own server (BYOS), with encryption enabled by default, and a 99.9% uptime service-level agreement (SLA) Compliance: Supports GDPR-aligned data deletion requests alongside long-term retention How Does AvePoint’s Google Workspace Backup Compare to Native Recovery? AvePoint’s Google Workspace backup differs from native recovery and Google Vault most in what each is actually built for: Native recovery windows last only a matter of days, and Vault manages retention and compliance without keeping a separate copy, while AvePoint keeps an independent, immutable, restorable copy on its own schedule. Capability Google Workspace Native / Vault AvePoint Purpose Retention and eDiscovery; not designed as a backup Independent backup and recovery, purpose-built Recovery window Admin console: about 25 days for deleted Drive or Gmail data, about 30 days for Contacts or Calendar events (Trash), about 20 days to recover a deleted user's full account Unlimited cloud storage; not capped to a native trash window Independent copy No, Vault keeps no independent copy of data Yes; backups are stored across more than a dozen global AvePoint data centers Restore to end users Very limited restore options directly to end users Granular or bulk restore via the ReCenter portal, self-service External/linked content Files indirectly shared with a user via an alias or Google Group (rather than directly) may not be held Covered as part of the Drive and Shared Drive backup, including permissions Backup frequency Not a scheduled, customer-managed backup Automated, up to 4 times a day Can One Platform Back Up Both Google Workspace and Microsoft 365? Yes, and you don’t need a separate backup tool for each environment. Many organizations run Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 side by side, whether through M&A, regional teams, or gradual migration, and both carry native-recovery gaps of their own. Treating them as separate backup problems misses the point: AvePoint backs up Google Workspace alongside Microsoft 365, Salesforce, and other SaaS applications on a single platform, so retention and restore are managed from a single console rather than a separate tool per environment. How Does AI Change the Stakes of Google Workspace Data Loss? AI raises the stakes because data loss becomes invisible and scaled. As organizations connect Gemini and other AI tools to Gmail, Drive, and Calendar, a gap in that data, a wiped folder, a deleted thread, no longer inconveniences just one person. It silently changes what the AI assistant retrieves and cites, so every answer built on that data can be quietly incomplete or wrong, with no error flagging it. This is a shift in what data loss costs. It used to surface as a personal productivity problem, one person noticing a missing file. Now, once AI assistants search and summarize across that same email and file data, the same gap reaches everyone who relies on their answers. Google Workspace Backup Maturity Tiers Tier What It Looks Like Tier 1: Native only Relying solely on Google’s trash and retention windows (~25 days) and Google Vault for eDiscovery; data lives only in Google Workspace, with no independent copy to restore from Tier 2: Partial coverage Native retention supplemented by manual exports for a few critical mailboxes or drive; no automation and no granular self-service restore Tier 3: AvePoint-backed, multi-platform Automated backup with granular and bulk restore, unlimited storage independent of Google’s own systems, and coverage extended across Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Salesforce under one platform AvePoint backs up Google Workspace alongside Microsoft 365, Salesforce, and other SaaS applications under one platform, with granular restore and unlimited storage independent of Google’s own systems. Frequently Asked Questions Does Google Vault back up Google Workspace data? No. Google Vault is a retention and eDiscovery tool. It only retains data stored within Google Workspace. It keeps no independent copy of your data and offers very limited and manual options for restoring content directly to end users. Does Google Vault cover all Workspace data types? No. Contacts is not a supported service in Vault, so it can’t be retained, held, or exported. It is recoverable only through short native windows. Does AvePoint’s Google Workspace backup replace native recovery or work alongside it? AvePoint’s Google Workspace backup works alongside Google’s native tools, providing the independent, restorable copy that Google Vault and Admin console retention were never designed to be. What does Google Workspace backup mean for Microsoft 365 recovery? Microsoft 365 carries native-recovery limitations of its own. AvePoint backs up both platforms under one platform, so recovery isn’t managed separately per environment. How often should I test a Google Workspace restore? Test a Google Workspace restore at least quarterly, and align the schedule to an organization’s audit or compliance review cycle so recovery evidence stays current. title: 3 Metrics to Help You Measure AI’s Impact
summary: For CFOs, the question is no longer whether AI is entering the enterprise, but whether the growing investment behind it is translating into measurable business value.
body_text: 3 Metrics to Help You Measure AI’s Impact Share: Copied! Artificial intelligence in software development has moved rapidly from experimentation to enterprise-wide deployment. Coding assistants, automated documentation, AI-powered testing, and intelligent development tools are now embedded in the daily workflows of many engineering teams. At the same time, organizations are expanding AI initiatives far beyond traditional IT functions while also raising expectations from business leaders who want faster delivery, greater automation, broader adoption, and real business outcomes. For CFOs, the question is no longer whether AI is entering the enterprise, but whether the growing investment behind it is translating into measurable business value. This surge in demand is placing substantial pressure on AI development teams. Rather than supporting a handful of pilot projects, developers are now expected to deliver and maintain AI capabilities across multiple business functions simultaneously. AI can significantly increase activity and output, but more projects, more code, and more automation do not automatically translate into better business results. As AI demand spreads across functions, leaders need a clearer way to separate useful acceleration from activity that simply adds complexity. The most useful place to start is with three questions. Are teams delivering customer-visible improvements more quickly? Is quality holding steady or improving? And is AI freeing up capacity for higher-value work and improved decision making? Three Ways Leaders Can Tell If AI is Really Working The metrics you choose need to be owned at the leadership level. Measurement that doesn’t connect to a business outcome is noise. While the right mix will vary by organization, most metrics fall into three categories that matter regardless of industry or scale. The first metric to consider is speed. How quickly are teams delivering valuable enhancements? It’s not just about moving faster for the sake of speed, but about accelerating the journey from concept to deployment in a way that provides real benefits to users. When AI empowers engineers to turn ideas into releases more efficiently, it enables earlier feedback, faster learning cycles, and a more direct route from investment to tangible business outcomes. The second metric to focus on is quality. Faster output is only valuable if the results maintain high standards. Leaders should watch for signs that reliability is stable or improving, such as a reduction in defects reaching customers, fewer preventable incidents, and decreased need for engineering rework. If AI increases speed but leads to more downstream issues, the supposed benefits will quickly be overwhelmed by costly setbacks. The third metric to evaluate is capacity. AI handles tasks such as drafting, summarizing, triaging, and other repetitive engineering work — but how are skilled teams using this newly freed time? The greatest benefits come from creating space for innovation, implementing customer-facing enhancements, and pursuing initiatives that drive true competitive advantage. In many organizations, these opportunities for higher-value work are the most significant return on AI investment. These three metrics of speed, quality, and capacity give leaders a practical way to judge whether AI is changing outcomes rather than just increasing activity. They are simple enough to use in business conversations and strong enough to support better investment decisions. Governance Must Be on the Front Lines Trust is essential for success, making it critical that AI be governed by well-defined guardrails for data usage, review, and validation. As agents enter production, the criticality rises, so leaders should establish usage policies before they’re needed, not after an incident forces the issue. That means four things: Governance: Agents operate within defined policy boundaries that include controls over model access, permitted actions, and audit trails. This is what gives leaders the confidence to expand adoption without losing control. Reviewable: Agent activity is visible and surfaced into the workflows where developers already work. When a developer can see, understand, and override what an agent has done, the system has integrity. Accountable: Human judgment is the check at every critical junction. Agents write the code, open the pull request, run the tests — a human approves the merge. Aligned to outcomes: Governance and measurement must be connected. The audit trail only has value tied to the business objectives you defined at the outset. Together, these four principles turn governance from a blocker into the foundation that makes scaling AI possible. What Leaders Should Take Away For leadership teams, measuring the impact of AI in software development isn’t about throwing around numbers and technical details. It’s about gaining clear insight into whether the organization is becoming more efficient, more dependable, and better at focusing employees on high-value activities. These are the improvements that drive lasting competitiveness. The greatest advantages from AI won’t go to organizations with the most pilot projects, but to those that can confidently articulate in a straightforward manner where AI is producing meaningful results and take decisive action based on that evidence. If you can measure whether AI is making teams faster, quality stronger, and capacity greater, you can make better decisions about what to scale, what to fix, and what to stop. title: Navigating SAMA, ADGM & DFSA Requirements with Teleport
summary: Learn how Teleport helps CSPs meet SAMA, ADGM, and DFSA compliance.
body_text: Read this article to learn: How SAMA's Cyber Security Framework, ADGM's Cyber Risk Management Rules, and the DFSA Rulebook define identity, access, and audit trail expectations for cloud service providers. How long-lived credentials, VPNs, bastions, and platform-specific access controls can make governance difficult to centralize and demonstrate to regulators. How a unified identity layer helps CSPs operationalize controls without sacrificing the agility sovereign cloud environments demand. The Middle East, especially the UAE and Saudi Arabia, has become a priority market for cloud service providers (CSPs) as governments accelerate digital transformation across public and private sectors. The opportunity is real, but so is the complexity. In our work with clients and regulators, Coalfire has seen that market entry often hinges less on commercial certifications and more on meeting strict data sovereignty and cybersecurity requirements. Many CSPs built their go-to-market models around a familiar split: commercial cloud offerings optimized for speed, scale, and feature velocity, and public sector offerings designed for higher security baselines, tighter operational controls, and reduced data movement. That distinction is starting to blur in Western markets as regulations like NIS2 expand baseline security expectations and modernization efforts such as FedRAMP 20x push for faster qualification of commercial solutions. In the Gulf, regulators have taken a centralized and national approach to cybersecurity and data governance from the outset, especially in sensitive sectors such as financial services. That has raised the bar for data localization, operational control, and access security. For CSPs, this creates a new challenge: success in these markets requires more self-contained, region-specific architectures than the commercial cloud patterns they have used elsewhere. From a continuous compliance perspective, this challenge also extends to how identities, privileged access, third-party access, and audit evidence are managed across region-specific environments. Traditional patterns built around long-lived credentials, VPNs, bastions, and platform-specific access controls can make that governance difficult to centralize and even harder to demonstrate. This is where a unified identity and access layer becomes strategically important. Meeting Kingdom of Saudi Arabia SAMA requirements The Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA) is Saudi Arabia’s central bank and a primary financial-sector regulator, overseeing banks, insurers, financing companies, credit bureaus, and financial market infrastructure. Its Cyber Security Framework (CSF) establishes cybersecurity expectations for these regulated Member Organizations. The CSF draws on established industry and international standards, including NIST, ISF, ISO, Basel, and PCI. It combines governance, risk management, identity and access management, operational security, third-party oversight, and measurable control effectiveness. Importantly for cloud service providers, the framework also establishes a strong data-location expectation: Member Organizations should use cloud services located in Saudi Arabia unless they obtain explicit approval from SAMA to use services outside the Kingdom. Specific to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) domain, the guidelines within section 3.3.5 are clear to emphasize systematic solutions that support centralization, automation, MFA for remote access and privileged access, and a comprehensive audit trail for IAM activities. Further, the CSF has defined (within section 3.3.13) MFA enforcement for a slew of service user activities, starting with basic registration and sign-on. Above all, the CSF requires strong, metrics-driven effectiveness measurement by organizations throughout its narrative, making the case for an agile, programmatic approach to identity management. Meeting United Arab Emirates FSRA and DFSA requirements A major financial hub connecting the EU, Asia and Africa, the UAE has consistently promoted business friendly environments that greatly attract FinTech ventures. With the advancements in digital banking, the country’s two premier “financial free zones” have established strict cybersecurity requirements commensurate with industry best practices. The Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) is highly competitive in digital assets, FinTech, and requires regulated operators to demonstrate strong Cyber Risk Management activities prescribed by its regulator, the Financial Services Regulatory Authority (FSRA). On the topic of protecting ICT assets, the framework recommends centralized and automated access management (3.5.7), overseen by a designated individual. ADGM expects firms to manage access through approval workflows, least privilege, prompt revocation, and recurring access reviews, while also treating privileged accounts with extra care – the assignment of a unique identifier, rather than privilege escalation to a regular operations account. Specifically, the framework also calls for strong authentication, MFA for internet-facing systems and privileged access, and encryption for user-to-system communications (3.5.8). The regulator emphasizes the need for demonstrable evidence for access risk mitigation activities, placing the onus on operators to approach IAM strategically. The Dubai International Financial Center (DIFC) is a longer established zone, hence featuring a deep, mature ecosystem for traditional banking, wealth management, and FinTech. The regulator DFSA urges member organizations to establish a Cyber Risk Management framework consulting well known standards from ISO, NIST, Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) and the CIS. DFSA expects firms to manage user access through formal approval, least-privilege assignment, prompt revocation, and regular access reviews, including detection of dormant or excessive accounts (5.5.8). DFSA also calls for MFA on all internet-accessible systems and privileged access, plus encrypted communication between users and systems (5.5.9). Like the ADGM, the DFSA also wants firms to separate admin activity from normal business use and keep privileged rights tightly limited. How Teleport supports compliance in Saudi Arabia and the UAE As a global compliance advisory and engineering firm, Coalfire is a trusted name that builds sovereign cloud solutions embedded with automation, programmatic management capabilities and latest security technologies/practices. Where strict data localization requirements are mandated, Coalfire packages environment specific IAM solutions that can help federate multiple sources, apply comprehensive access control requirements, and maintain a rigorous audit posture with Teleport. A unified identity layer Teleport provides a unified identity layer for managing users, assets, AI agents, and machines across cloud, on-premises, or hybrid infrastructure, treating each as a first class identity while streamlining Single Sign On (SSO), MFA, Role Based Access Control (RBAC) and Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC). Device Trust policies support formal authorization, least privilege, and identity attribution across the enterprise, rather than being limited to cloud tenancy. Just-in-time access and eliminating standing privileges Extending administrative functions to support Infrastructure as code (IaC), Teleport is tailormade for agile cloud environments that are managed programmatically. Access Requests provide Just-in-Time (JIT) elevation and approval workflows for sensitive infrastructure, while per-session MFA, short-lived X.509 certificates , passwordless authentication, and automatic expiry eliminate standing privileges, shared credentials, and long-lived SSH keys — high risk elements within a sensitive data storage environment. Read this guide to learn more about short-lived certificates for financial infrastructure: Certificate-Based Authentication for Payment & Banking Infrastructure Consistent controls across infrastructure Teleport applies these controls consistently across servers, databases, Kubernetes clusters, cloud consoles, internal applications, and desktops, with resource-level policies that help limit lateral movement and control third-party access. Teleport’s Machine & Workload Identity extends the same model to service accounts, CI/CD pipelines, workloads, and AI agents through short-lived, automatically renewable credentials. Automatic detection and enrollment of infrastructure resources A frequently underserved area within IAM solutions is continuous inventory management. Teleport’s unified inventory and auto-discovery provides increased visibility into protected infrastructure and can be used to map identities to assets. These features help organizations understand the threat landscape from an unauthorized access lens. Automatic access reviews and identity locking support timely revocation and periodic governance for dynamic environments, where traditional human lead reviews are simply unscalable. Audit-ready visibility Session recording , live session monitoring, detailed and centralized event logs across resources, and SIEM integrations create evidence for access requests, approvals, privileged activity, and security monitoring. Compliance beyond data sovereignty For cloud service providers entering the Gulf’s regulated financial markets, compliance is not simply a matter of where data is stored and encrypted. There is great emphasis on how access is granted, protected, monitored, and evidenced across the environments that process critical data. SAMA, ADGM, and DFSA each articulate this expectation within their guidelines, and the common theme is that organizations need stronger control over identities, privileged access, third parties, and continuous auditability to minimize access risks. Teleport can help CSPs operationalize these controls through a unified identity layer, supporting secure access without sacrificing the agility required to operate sovereign cloud environments. Accelerate KSA and UAE compliance Learn how Teleport helps organizations around the world accelerate compliance and simplify audits with unified identity, zero trust, and identity-traceable audit trails.

title: 811 Day is a reminder to call before you dig into your next project
summary: April is National Safe Digging Month, a perfect time to revisit a critical message: Before you put a shovel in the ground, remember to contact 811 first.
body_text: April is Safe Digging Month, a perfect time to revisit a critical message: Before you put a shovel in the ground, remember to contact 811 first. Damaging or striking a utility line can be a dangerous situation that causes property damage, fines, service disruptions, serious injury or even death. Don’t let a dig mistake become a big mistake. Call 811 or visit call811.com first. It’s free, easy to set up, and everything you need to know for your state’s requirements is handled in one contact. It’s also the law. Make it a habit Contacting 811 before digging to locate buried lines should be everyone’s habit. Find your state’s wait time and call center link below: Colorado (three days): co811.org Michigan (three days): missdig.net Minnesota (two days): gopherstateonecall.org New Mexico (two days): nm811.org North Dakota (three days): ndonecall.com South Dakota (two days): sdonecall.com Texas (two days): texas811.org Wisconsin (three days): diggershotline.com Did you know? Customer-owned lines you’ve installed in your yard for a gas grill or electricity in a shed or garage, for example, are your responsibility. Use a licensed plumbing, heating or electrical contractor to locate them prior to digging and to maintain them. What you don’t know can hurt you. The depth of utility lines will never be indicated. Depth also changes over time with erosion, storms, floods, soil condition, heaving from frost and changes to landscape. Some utilities, such as cable companies, are notorious for burying their lines very shallow. Cross boring, for example, happens without the homeowner’s permission. Natural gas smells like rotten eggs. Natural gas in its original state has no odor. But we add an odorant to the natural gas, called mercaptan, to help you recognize a gas leak. It smells like rotten eggs to many, but it may smell differently to you. If you nick a gas line, clear the area quickly. Once safely away, call 911 and Xcel Energy to investigate and repair the damage. Do not use anything that could create a spark (such as lighters, matches, light switches, garage door openers, ignition switches or even cellphones). Hand digging. Before you can safely work close to or across an underground utility line, you must first dig by hand to expose the line and verify its exact location and depth. Be knowledgeable about the hand-digging tolerance zone laws in your state. Always assume powerlines are energized. Be especially mindful after a storm. Even if there are no sparks or sound, that doesn’t mean the powerline is not energized. Always look up for overhead powerlines and stay at least 20 feet away from them. Consider what’s overhead and underground before planting anything that could possibly grow into electric or natural gas lines. Stop for stop tape. Gas and electric lines are sometimes buried below yellow (gas) or red (electric) warning tape. If you encounter stop tape, stop digging and hand dig to fully expose the line and verify its exact location and depth before you continue your project. Find more information and valuable tips for safe digging at Xcel Energy/Public Safety/call-before-you-dig .

title: How to Permanently Turn Off Prepaid Electricity Meter Beeping Sound
summary: Annoyed by your prepaid electricity meter beeping? Learn how to permanently turn off the beeping sound with easy, step-by-step methods anyone can follow.
body_text: Travel Tips You’re finally drifting off to sleep, the room is quiet, and then… beep. beep. beep. Your prepaid electricity meter starts chirping like it has something urgent to say at midnight. Sound familiar? If you’ve ever lived with a prepaid electricity token meter, you know exactly how maddening that sound can be. Whether it’s a low-credit alert, a confirmation beep after entering a token, or just a random notification, the noise can seriously disrupt your peace at home. The good news? You’re not stuck with it. Many people, from renters to homeowners, especially those living abroad or managing properties remotely (like many in the Indonesian diaspora ), deal with this exact issue. This guide walks you through how to permanently turn off your prepaid electricity meter beeping sound, step by step, in plain language. List of Content Toggle Why Does Your Prepaid Electricity Meter Keep Beeping? Before you silence it, it helps to know why it’s making noise in the first place. Prepaid electricity meters (also called token meters or KWh meters) are designed to alert you through sound for several reasons. 1. Low Credit Warning The most common cause of that persistent beeping is a low credit balance . When your electricity credit drops below a certain threshold, the meter beeps repeatedly to warn you that you’re running low and need to top up soon. 2. Token Entry Confirmation When you enter a new electricity token code, the meter beeps to confirm the entry was accepted. This is a one-time sound and usually stops on its own after a few seconds. 3. Tamper or Error Alerts Some meters beep when they detect unusual activity, a wiring issue, or an internal error. This type of beeping usually comes with an error code on the display screen. 4. Default Factory Sound Setting Some meter models simply have the sound turned on by default from the manufacturer. Even without any alerts, certain meters emit periodic sounds as part of their standard operation, and this can be adjusted or disabled. How to Permanently Turn Off the Beeping Sound on Your Prepaid Meter The method you use will depend on your meter’s brand and model. The most widely used prepaid electricity meters in Southeast Asia include brands like Itron , Hexing , Landis+Gyr , and Star . Each has slightly different button combinations, but the logic is similar across models. Here’s how to approach it. 1. Try the Standard Button Combination Method Many prepaid meters allow you to toggle the sound off through a simple keypad sequence. The most commonly reported method that works on several popular models is entering 812 followed by the Enter or Accept button. Some models respond to pressing and holding the Enter button for 5 to 10 seconds. After doing this, the display may briefly show a confirmation like “SOUND OFF” or the beeping will simply stop. 2. Use the Code Specific to Your Meter Brand Different brands use different codes to access the sound settings. Here’s a quick reference for common meters: Itron meters: Press 812 + Enter to toggle the alarm sound on or off. Hexing meters: Try pressing 812 + Enter or hold the backlight/function button for several seconds. Landis+Gyr meters: Check the meter display for a menu option using the scroll button. Some models have a dedicated sound menu. Star (Bintang) meters: Use 456 + Enter or consult the user manual as this brand varies by firmware version. If none of these work immediately, try the sequence a couple of times. Some meters require the input twice to confirm the change. 3. Check the Manual or Label on Your Meter Your meter may have a small sticker with a model number. Take note of it and search for the specific user manual online. The manufacturer’s official guide will list the exact keypad sequence for sound settings. This is especially useful if your meter is a less common model. 4. Contact Your Electricity Provider If you’ve tried all the button combinations and nothing works, your next step is to call your electricity provider’s customer service line . In Indonesia, that would be PLN. In other countries, it’s your local state or private power utility. Explain that you want to disable the meter’s alarm sound, and they can either walk you through the process over the phone or send a technician to help. This is the safest option if you’re unsure about pressing unfamiliar codes on your meter. 5. Request a Technician Visit for Persistent Issues If the beeping is caused by an error code or a tamper alert rather than just the default sound setting, you should not try to silence it through button presses alone. This type of beeping may signal a real problem with the meter. Request an official technician visit to inspect and resolve the issue properly before attempting to mute any alerts. Things to Keep in Mind Before You Disable the Sound Turning off your meter’s beeping sound is generally harmless if done correctly, but there are a few things worth keeping in mind so you don’t accidentally create a bigger problem. 1. Don’t Ignore the Low Credit Alert Entirely If you disable the beeping, make sure you have another way to monitor your electricity credit. Many providers now offer apps or SMS notifications to track your balance. Set a reminder to top up regularly so you don’t get caught off-guard with no power. Silencing the meter doesn’t mean your credit situation changes. 2. Never Tamper with the Meter’s Internal Components Some DIY forums suggest physically disconnecting a buzzer inside the meter. Do not do this. Opening the meter casing is illegal in most countries and can void warranties, trigger tampering alerts, or even cause electrical hazards. Always stick to the approved keypad method or contact your provider. 3. The Sound Might Reset After a Power Outage On some older meter models, the sound setting resets to the default (on) after a power interruption. If this happens to you, simply re-enter the same code sequence after the power comes back on. It’s a minor inconvenience, but good to know in advance. Managing Electricity Costs as an Expat or Overseas Worker If you’re an expat or migrant worker helping a family member back home manage utility bills remotely, staying on top of electricity tokens can be tricky from overseas. Many families in Indonesia and other parts of Southeast Asia rely on prepaid meters, and topping up remotely requires sending money home in a reliable, timely way. Understanding local utility systems, including how to manage and silence those alert sounds, helps you give better guidance to your family even from thousands of kilometers away. Being aware of local living costs, like electricity bills, also ties into broader financial awareness. For instance, if you’re based in Australia or Singapore, understanding your own tax and income situation helps you plan how much to send home. Knowing about income tax in Australia or the Singapore income tax rate can help you budget smarter for both local expenses and international support. title: Full Speed with Dad
summary: At Road America, a Father’s Day weekend at the XPEL GP proves how racing can create lasting memories, connect generations, and bring families closer.
body_text: Father’s Day at Full Speed Some things hit differently when you see them through someone else's eyes. That's the quiet magic that unfolded at Road America this Father's Day, when XPEL welcomed Brian Jannusch – Wisconsin-raised JDM importer and automotive influencer – and his father to this year’s XPEL Grand Prix INDYCAR race at Road America. For Brian, it was a weekend at one of America's greatest race tracks. For his dad, it was something far bigger: a first. A Father's Day Worth Remembering Brian Jannusch has spent years immersed in car culture. From importing Japanese domestic market vehicles to building a loyal following online, cars aren't just a hobby – they’re a way of life. But watching his dad step onto the grounds of Road America for the very first time? That was something new entirely. "He's always known I love cars, but he'd never really seen what this world looks like up close," Brian said. "Bringing him here on Father's Day, watching his face when he heard the engines – that was the whole trip for me." His father, Patrick Galewarts, didn't need long to find his footing. Within minutes of arriving, the noise, the smell of racing fuel, the crowd buzzing with anticipation – it all clicked. "I didn't know what to expect," Patrick admitted. "But the moment I saw the camaraderie amongst the teams – and the fans – and those cars came around the first corner, I understood. I get it now. I completely get it." Seeing Racing for the First Time There's a particular kind of joy that belongs only to first-timers. Unfiltered. Unguarded. You can't fake it, and you can't manufacture it. Brian's father had it in spades. The people. The cars. The kids and laughter. The tailgating. And the speed… oh the speed. The father who had watched his son talk about cars for decades was, for the first time, living inside the world his son had always described – and loving every second of it. That's what the XPEL Grand Prix at Road America does. It doesn't just put on a race. It creates moments that stick. Road America: A Track Unlike Any Other Nestled in the rolling hills of Elkhart Lake, Wisconsin, roughly an hour north of Milwaukee, Road America isn’t just another race venue. It's a 4.048-mile natural road course that has hosted world-class motorsport since 1955. The facility is massive – fans can walk the grounds freely, exploring corner by corner, claiming a patch of grass wherever the view suits them best. Campers line the perimeter. Tailgates stretch as far as you can see. Chainsaw sculptures dot the grounds like quirky landmarks you didn't know you needed. Road America has a texture that modern racing facilities often lack – it feels lived-in, beloved, and entirely its own. The IndyCar racing itself delivered. A late caution near the finish kept the crowd on edge, the kind of race-ending tension that reminds you why motorsport has a stranglehold on its fans. For a first-timer watching it all unfold, it was the perfect introduction. When Racing Brings People Together XPEL has been a fixture at Road America for years, and the XPEL Grand Prix has grown into one of the marquee events on the IndyCar calendar. Hosting Brian and his father on Father's Day wasn't just a hospitality moment – it was a reminder of what the best motorsport experiences are built on: access, atmosphere, and the chance to share something real with someone you love. The cars are fast. The racing is fierce. But the stories that outlast any single race are the ones about the people watching it. Brian Jannusch will remember plenty from this Father's Day – the IndyCar engines echoing through the Wisconsin hills, the late drama on track, the sprawling beauty of Road America in summer. But most of all, he'll remember the look on his dad's face when it all made sense for the first time. "Road America has always been special to me — it's in my blood, it's home," Brian said. "But getting to share it with my dad, on Father's Day, at a track right here in Wisconsin? That's something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life. You can't plan a moment like that. It just happens, and you're grateful you were there for it." That's the thing about racing. Done right, it doesn't just win over fans. It connects generations.

title: Takeaways From The Forrester Wave™: Data Lakehouses, Q3 2026
summary: The enterprise data lakehouse is evolving. Once designed primarily to consolidate data for analytics, today’s lakehouse has become the operational foundation for agentic AI, delivering the trusted, governed, and real-time data that intelligent agents require to reason and act. As AI shifts from generating insights to executing business processes, organizations must rethink what they expect […]
body_text: The enterprise data lakehouse is evolving. Once designed primarily to consolidate data for analytics, today’s lakehouse has become the operational foundation for agentic AI, delivering the trusted, governed, and real-time data that intelligent agents require to reason and act. As AI shifts from generating insights to executing business processes, organizations must rethink what they expect from their lakehouse platform. This evolution redefines vendor evaluation, prioritizing AI readiness, trust, openness, and operational intelligence over storage and query performance. New Lakehouse Capabilities Support Agentic Use Cases To help organizations navigate this shift, Forrester evaluated 14 leading lakehouse vendors in The Forrester Wave™: Data Lakehouses, Q3 2026 . The evaluation reflects the changing role of the lakehouse in the AI era and identifies the capabilities that will distinguish platforms capable of supporting enterprise-scale agentic AI. While traditional data management capabilities remain important, the report makes it clear that future-ready lakehouses must also serve as the execution layer for AI-driven applications. The key takeaways from the evaluation are that: The lakehouse is becoming an execution layer for agentic AI. The data lakehouse is no longer limited to storing and serving data for analytics. Instead, it must continuously provide trusted, governed, real-time context that AI agents can use to reason, decide, and act. This shift fundamentally changes how organizations should evaluate vendors. Rather than prioritizing storage-centric capabilities alone, buyers should assess how effectively a lakehouse supports AI-native workloads, real-time operations, and integration with enterprise AI ecosystems. Trust is the foundation of an AI-ready lakehouse. As AI agents increasingly make autonomous decisions, weaknesses in data quality, governance, lineage, or security become execution risks rather than analytical limitations. Organizations should prioritize lakehouse platforms that embed governance, automated lineage, fine-grained access controls, continuous data quality monitoring, and policy enforcement as core platform capabilities. Open architectures are critical for long-term AI success. AI is evolving rapidly, requiring organizations to integrate multiple models, orchestration frameworks, cloud environments, and data services. Lakehouses built on open table formats, interoperable metadata standards, extensible APIs, and zero-copy data sharing provide the flexibility needed to adapt while reducing vendor lock-in. Vendor evaluations should therefore consider ecosystem interoperability and architectural openness as strategic differentiators rather than optional features. AI enablement is the new competitive differentiator for lakehouse platforms. Storage, scalability, and query performance have become table stakes. Today, lakehouses distinguish themselves by delivering real-time context, semantic intelligence, vector-native capabilities, and AI-ready data services that enable autonomous agents to retrieve, reason, and act on enterprise data. Organizations should evaluate vendors based on how effectively their platforms operationalize AI, as this capability will define enterprise value and competitive advantage in the next generation of data platforms.
